In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

live_data_statements: The sample comprised 262 adolescents diagnosed with CD who were enrolled in a larger NIMH-funded longitudinal study (R01MH123535: PI Thomson).

To assess changes in perceived belonging, competence, and meaningful existence following each Interact VR condition, participants completed an adapted version of the Cyberball Need-Threat Scale (NTS; Williams & Jarvis, 2006).
Participants were recruited by trained research coordinators from a Level 1 Trauma Center in Virginia.

Participants were fitted with a VR headset and completed a brief orientation to the virtual environment during which they were asked to describe the surroundings to confirm adequate visualization and familiarize themselves with the immersive environment before the experimental task began.
Next, participants completed Interact VR, an immersive social interaction paradigm adapted from the Cyberball task (Williams & Jarvis, 2006).
Participants completed three experimental conditions representing varying levels of social inclusion.

Immediately following each condition, participants completed self-report measures assessing perceived social regard (i.e., how much they liked the virtual players and how much they believed the virtual players liked them), belonging, competence, meaningful existence, valence, arousal, control, and six emotions.
Participants were most likely to report anger during the severe exclusion condition.

As social exclusion increased, participants had a progressively greater probability of reporting sadness, anger, and disgust, alongside reduced happiness, demonstrating that increasing social exclusion elicited distinct patterns of emotional responding.
However, because the subtle and severe exclusion conditions were randomized, differences between these conditions are less likely to reflect sequence effects.

Social exclusion is a powerful social stressor because acceptance and belonging are fundamental human needs (Baumeister & Leary, 1995).

text.text: Even brief experiences of exclusion can produce immediate changes in affect, perceived social regard, and satisfaction of fundamental psychological needs, including belonging, control, self-esteem, and meaningful existence (Gerber & Wheeler, 2009; Nida & Williams, 2017; Richman & Leary, 2009; Williams, 2009; Zadro et al., 2004).

text.text: These responses are particularly important during adolescence, a developmental period characterized by heightened sensitivity to peer evaluation, social acceptance, and affiliation (Blakemore & Mills, 2014; Crone & Dahl, 2012; Somerville, 2013).

text.text: Prior research has demonstrated that social exclusion influences adolescents' mood, satisfaction of fundamental psychological needs, and neural systems involved in social evaluation and distress (Masten et al., 2009; Ruggieri et al., 2013; Sebastian et al., 2010).

text.text: Consequently, adolescence represents a critical developmental period for investigating how young people perceive and respond to social exclusion.

Among adolescents, understanding responses to social exclusion may be particularly important in youth with conduct disorder (CD), a common and highly impairing neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by persistent patterns of aggressive, antisocial, and rule-breaking behavior that disrupt social, academic, and occupational functioning (Fairchild et al., 2019).

text.text: Interpersonal difficulties are prominent among adolescents with CD, who experience disproportionately high rates of peer rejection, victimization, and relationship instability (Baumann et al., 2023; Girard et al., 2024).

text.text: Importantly, these social experiences are likely to be reciprocal, as peer rejection can both contribute to and result from aggressive and antisocial behavior across development (Dodge et al., 2003; Girard et al., 2024; Robertson et al., 2023).

text.text: Although substantial progress has been made in understanding the neurocognitive, emotional, and developmental characteristics of youth with CD (Blair, 2013; Blair & Zhang, 2020; Frick et al., 2014; Frick & Kemp, 2021), CD is characterized by substantial heterogeneity in its clinical presentation and similar behavioral manifestations may not reflect uniform cognitive and emotional functioning across affected youth (Fairchild et al., 2019; Kohls et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Although substantial progress has been made in understanding the neurocognitive, emotional, and developmental characteristics of youth with CD <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Blair, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Blair & Zhang, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Frick et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Frick & Kemp, 2021)</ref>, CD is characterized by substantial heterogeneity in its clinical presentation and similar behavioral manifestations may not reflect uniform cognitive and emotional functioning across affected youth <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Fairchild et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Kohls et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Despite advances in characterizing differences in emotion processing and related neurocognitive functions, comparatively little is known about how adolescents with CD subjectively experience and respond to socially meaningful interpersonal interactions.

Social exclusion provides a particularly informative interpersonal context for addressing this gap because it directly challenges processes that are fundamental to peer relationships such as social acceptance and belonging.

Understanding how adolescents with CD perceive and affectively respond to varying experiences of social exclusion may therefore provide important insight into the social-affective processes underlying their interpersonal functioning.
Addressing this gap requires experimental paradigms capable of systematically creating experiences of social exclusion under controlled conditions.

To date, research on social exclusion has relied predominantly on the Cyberball paradigm (Williams et al., 2000; Williams & Jarvis, 2006), in which participants believe they are playing an online ball-tossing game with other individuals who are experimentally programmed to include or exclude them.

text.text: Owing to its brevity, standardization, experimental control, and ease of implementation, Cyberball has become the most widely used experimental paradigm for investigating social exclusion (Vanhollebeke et al., 2023; Williams & Jarvis, 2006).
text.formatted: Owing to its brevity, standardization, experimental control, and ease of implementation, Cyberball has become the most widely used experimental paradigm for investigating social exclusion <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Vanhollebeke et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Williams & Jarvis, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Across child and adolescent clinical and community samples, Cyberball research has consistently demonstrated that even brief experiences of exclusion threaten fundamental psychological needs including belonging, control, self-esteem, and meaningful existence, and influence emotional, cognitive, and behavioral responses to social interactions (Hartgerink et al., 2015; Masten et al., 2009; Sebastian et al., 2010; Vanhollebeke et al., 2023; Williams, 2009).

text.text: Despite this extensive evidence base, investigations of social exclusion in adolescents with CD remain comparatively limited.

Consequently, it remains unclear whether established paradigms can effectively characterize how adolescents with CD perceive and respond to social exclusion or distinguish responses across varying degrees of exclusion.

More broadly, extending experimental paradigms for social exclusion provides opportunities for developmentally appropriate and ecologically valid assessment of multiple dimensions of social-affective functioning.

This emphasis is consistent with recommendations from the National Institute of mental Health's (NIMH) National Advisory Mental Health Council (NAMHC) Workgroup on the Research Domain Criteria (RDoC) framework (Cuthbert & Insel, 2013; Insel et al., 2010; Morris et al., 2022), which identified rejection sensitivity as a priority construct within the Social Processes domain and emphasized the importance of developing ecologically valid experimental paradigms capable of measuring dimensional variation in social processes across development (NAMHC Workgroup, 2016).

text.text: Although Cyberball was identified as a state-of-the-art paradigm for assessing rejection sensitivity, the NAMHC Workgroup ( 2016)also identified opportunities for its continued development, including greater dimensionality of outcomes, further evaluation across developmental and participant groups, and greater standardization, while more broadly emphasizing the need for measures of social processes that optimize ecological validity.

text.text: Building on these priorities, recent advances in immersive virtual reality (VR) offer a promising approach for developing experimental paradigms that measure multidimensional aspects of social-affective functioning within ecologically meaningful social interactions.

Unlike traditional computerized programs, immersive VR places participants within dynamic, reciprocal social environments that more closely approximate everyday peer interactions while maintaining experimental control.
Traditional Cyberball affords substantial experimental control but provides a more limited approximation of the perceptual immersion and social presence characteristic of everyday peer interactions.
Thus, immersive VR offers a complementary approach that preserves experimental control while increasing the ecological validity of experimentally induced social interactions.

Emerging evidence suggests that immersive VR paradigms can reliably elicit psychological and emotional responses to social exclusion similar to those observed with Cyberball, while providing greater realism and social presence (De Luca et al., 2026; Stallmann et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Emerging evidence suggests that immersive VR paradigms can reliably elicit psychological and emotional responses to social exclusion similar to those observed with Cyberball, while providing greater realism and social presence <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(De Luca et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Stallmann et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, VR also provides an opportunity to extend how social exclusion itself is experimentally represented.
Although Cyberball permits variation in the degree of social inclusion and exclusion, much of the literature has focused on the effects of ostracism relative to inclusion (Hartgerink et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Although Cyberball permits variation in the degree of social inclusion and exclusion, much of the literature has focused on the effects of ostracism relative to inclusion <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Hartgerink et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Yet exclusion in everyday interpersonal interactions can vary in degree, from relatively subtle reductions in social engagement to more overt exclusion.

Examining responses across varying levels of exclusion can clarify whether different dimensions of social-affective functioning change progressively with increasing social exclusion, emerge only at more pronounced levels of exclusion, or show distinct patterns of sensitivity across response domains.
VR provides the experimental flexibility to model varying levels of exclusion while assessing multiple dimensions of social-affective responding within an immersive interpersonal context.

To address the need for ecologically valid experimental paradigms for assessing multidimensional social-affective responses across varying levels of social exclusion, we developed Interact VR, an immersive VR paradigm adapted from Cyberball (Williams et al., 2000; Williams & Jarvis, 2006).
text.formatted: To address the need for ecologically valid experimental paradigms for assessing multidimensional social-affective responses across varying levels of social exclusion, we developed Interact VR, an immersive VR paradigm adapted from Cyberball <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Williams et al., 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Williams & Jarvis, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Building on prior applications of immersive VR to social exclusion (e.g., De Luca et al., 2026; Stallmann et al., 2023), Interact VR integrates an immersive Cyberball-inspired peer interaction with systematically varied levels of social exclusion and repeated within-person assessment across multiple dimensions of social-affective responding.
text.formatted: Building on prior applications of immersive VR to social exclusion (e.g., De <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Luca et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Stallmann et al., 2023)</ref>, Interact VR integrates an immersive Cyberball-inspired peer interaction with systematically varied levels of social exclusion and repeated within-person assessment across multiple dimensions of social-affective responding.

text.text: Specifically, Interact VR retains Cyberball's experimental control over peer inclusion and exclusion while placing adolescents in a dynamic virtual peer environment and assessing perceived social regard, fundamental psychological needs, affective responses, and discrete emotions following each experimental condition.

The present study sought to provide initial validation evidence for Interact VR in adolescents with CD by examining whether social-affective responses varied systematically with experimentally varied levels of social exclusion.
In so doing, we sought to characterize how youth with CD subjectively respond across multiple social-affective domains as exclusion became increasingly pronounced.
Specifically, we tested four hypotheses.

First, increasing exclusion severity was expected to be associated with lower perceived social regard, reflected in reduced perceptions of being liked by the virtual peers and lower liking of the virtual peers.
Second, increasing exclusion severity was expected to be associated with greater threat to belonging and meaningful existence.

Third, greater exclusion severity was expected to be associated with increasingly negative affective responses, reflected by lower affective valence and perceived control, whereas arousal was examined separately given its less predictable role during social stress.
Finally, increasing exclusion severity was expected to be associated with greater likelihood of experiencing sadness, anger, and disgust, lower likelihood of happiness.
Fear and surprise were examined as exploratory discrete emotions because theory and prior evidence provide less specific directional expectations for these responses in this context.
The sample comprised 262 adolescents diagnosed with CD who were enrolled in a larger NIMH-funded longitudinal study (R01MH123535: PI Thomson).
Participants ranged in age from 13 to 17 years (Mage = 15.75, SD = 1.28).
The sample was predominantly male (63.40%), with participants identifying as African American (57%), White (35%), American Indian or Alaska Native (1%), Asian (1%), or multiracial (6%).
Participants received $160 for their participation.
All study procedures were approved by the Virginia Commonwealth University Institutional Review Board.
Perceived social regard was assessed using four items assessing (a) how much participants thought Alex and Riley liked them and (b) how much participants liked Alex and Riley.
Items were rated on a 5-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (not at all) to 5 (very much).
Combining the two items demonstrated high internal reliability (via Spearman-Brown split-half correlations) during all three task conditions (Table 1).

text.text: To assess changes in perceived belonging, competence, and meaningful existence following each Interact VR condition, participants completed an adapted version of the Cyberball Need-Threat Scale (NTS; Williams & Jarvis, 2006).
text.formatted: To assess changes in perceived belonging, competence, and meaningful existence following each Interact VR condition, participants completed an adapted version of the Cyberball Need-Threat Scale (NTS; <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Williams & Jarvis, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: The adapted measure consisted of 12 items assessing the fundamental psychological needs of belonging (e.g., "I felt rejected," "I felt excluded by the other players"), competence (e.g., "I felt bad about myself," "I felt dissatisfied with how I played"), and meaningful existence (e.g., "I felt that I didn't matter," "I felt that it didn't make a difference that I was there"), with four items assessing each construct.
Items were rated on a 5-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (not at all) to 5 (extremely), with higher scores indicating greater threat to the corresponding psychological need.
Sum scores were calculated separately for each subscale.
All three subscales demonstrated good internal consistency via Cronbach's alpha across the Interact VR conditions (Table 1).
text.formatted: All three subscales demonstrated good internal consistency via Cronbach's alpha across the Interact VR conditions (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>).

text.text: To assess emotional responses following each Interact VR condition, participants selected emotions that best described how they felt after each condition.
Emotions included sadness, anger, surprise, fear, disgust, happiness.
Each emotion was scored dichotomously (0 = not endorsed,1 = endorsed) and analyzed separately.
To assess changes in subjective affect following each Interact VR condition, participants compelled the Subjective Emoji Affect Scale (SEAS; Kjærvik & Thomson, 2026).

text.text: The SEAS is a brief graphical self-report measure designed to assess three dimensions of affective experience: affective valence, subjective arousal, and perceived control.
The measure uses developmentally appropriate emoji-style visual anchors accompanied by brief text descriptors to facilitate selfreport in adolescent samples.

Participants rated each dimension using bi-polar 10-point visual scales immediately following each condition (e.g., "During the game, how did you feel from 1 (Simley & Happy), to 10 (Frowning & Unhappy)?").

text.text: Higher valence scores indicated more negative affective valence, higher arousal scores indicated greater subjective arousal, and higher control scores indicated greater perceived control.
Participants were recruited by trained research coordinators from a Level 1 Trauma Center in Virginia.
Adolescents who met study eligibility criteria and expressed interest in participating were scheduled for an in-person laboratory assessment.
Upon arrival, written informed assent and consent were obtained from adolescents and caregivers in separate rooms prior to participation.

Participants were fitted with a VR headset and completed a brief orientation to the virtual environment during which they were asked to describe the surroundings to confirm adequate visualization and familiarize themselves with the immersive environment before the experimental task began.
The research team simultaneously observed the VR display on an external monitor to ensure proper task presentation and recording throughout the session.
Participants first completed a 3-minute control condition in which they were instructed to sit quietly and relax while viewing a virtual room containing a fish tank.
Next, participants completed Interact VR, an immersive social interaction paradigm adapted from the Cyberball task (Williams & Jarvis, 2006).
text.formatted: Next, participants completed Interact VR, an immersive social interaction paradigm adapted from the Cyberball task <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Williams & Jarvis, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Within the three virtual environment conditions, participants believed they were playing a ball-tossing game with two other human participants, represented by computer-controlled avatars named Alex and Riley.
During each condition, participants tossed and received an "orb blast" with the avatars according to the programmed interaction sequence (Figure 1).
text.formatted: During each condition, participants tossed and received an "orb blast" with the avatars according to the programmed interaction sequence (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: The experimental manipulation involved systematically varying the number of orb blasts received by participants while keeping all other aspects of the interaction constant.
Participants completed three experimental conditions representing varying levels of social inclusion.
During the inclusion condition, participants received five orb tosses from the other players.
During the subtle exclusion condition, participants received four orb tosses, and during the severe exclusion condition, participants received only one orb toss.
The inclusion condition was always administered first to establish expectations of reciprocal interaction before participants experienced exclusion.

Presenting the inclusion condition first ensured that subsequent exclusion conditions represented a deviation from an established interaction pattern rather than an initially unfamiliar social environment.
The subtle and severe exclusion conditions were subsequently presented in randomized order to minimize order effects.
Each condition lasted approximately 3 minutes.

Immediately following each condition, participants completed self-report measures assessing perceived social regard (i.e., how much they liked the virtual players and how much they believed the virtual players liked them), belonging, competence, meaningful existence, valence, arousal, control, and six emotions.

To examine whether perceived social regard, belonging, competence, meaningful existence, and affective responses differed across the three Interact VR conditions, separate linear mixed-effects models were estimated for each continuous outcome, including feeling liked by the avatars, liking the avatars, belonging, competence, meaningful existence, valence, arousal, and control.
Condition was entered into model as a fixed within-subjects effect and participant intercepts were allowed to vary randomly.

Linear mixed-effects models were selected because they account for the within-subject dependence of repeated observations while accommodating incomplete repeated-measures data through maximum likelihood estimation.
Significant omnibus effects were followed by Holm-adjusted pairwise comparisons of estimated marginal means.
Raw scores were analyzed rather than change scores because the primary objective was to compare psychological responses across the three experimentally manipulated conditions.
We also examined a multilevel logistic regression model that estimated the effect of each condition on the probability of reporting each of the six emotions we measured.
Exploratory contrasts of emotion probabilities were tested using the Benjamin-Hochberg False Discovery Rate (FDR) correction.
Analyses were conducted in R (R Core Team, 2025).

text.text: Participants were most likely to report anger during the severe exclusion condition.

Our model-derived probabilities were such that anger had a 40% probability during the severe exclusion condition, relative to 9.45% and 2.15% in the subtle exclusion and inclusions conditions, respectively.
Disgust was also significantly more likely in the severe exclusion condition than in the subtle exclusion or inclusion conditions.

Happiness was significantly more likely during the inclusion condition with a predicted probability of 80.55% in contrast to the probability of happiness under the subtle, 58.00%, or severe, 15.33% exclusion conditions.

Sadness showed a similar pattern in the inverse, such that the severe exclusion condition carried the highest predicted probability of sadness, 19.42% relative to the subtle, 6.26%, or inclusion, 1.06% conditions.
However, fear and surprise were not significantly different across the condition comparisons.

The present study provides initial validation evidence for Interact VR, an immersive VR paradigm designed to examine multidimensional social-affective responses across varying levels of social exclusion in adolescents with CD.
Across three within-person conditions, increasing exclusion produced systematic changes across multiple domains of social-affective functioning.

Most outcomes, including feeling liked by the other 'players', belonging, meaningful existence, valence, control, and discrete emotions, distinguished inclusion, subtle exclusion, and severe exclusion, demonstrating strong condition sensitivity and construct-consistent response patterns.
However, not all domains responded uniformly.

Competence threat only differentiated severe exclusion from the other conditions, arousal decreased rather than increased as exclusion intensified, and the likelihood of experiencing fear and surprise did not vary by condition.

Together, these findings suggest that Interact VR captures expected and theoretically meaningful patterns of responding to varying levels of social exclusion, providing initial support for its use as an ecologically valid, experimentally controlled paradigm for investigating multidimensional social-affective functioning.

One of the principal findings of the present study was that adolescents with CD systematically distinguished among inclusion, subtle exclusion, and severe exclusion across multiple domains of social-affective functioning.

The effect of Interact VR condition was graded by the degree of exclusion which evoked lower perceptions of being liked by the task partners, reduced liking of the task partners, and greater threat to belonging, meaningful existence, and competence needs supporting evidence that even brief experiences of social exclusion disrupt fundamental psychological needs and alter interpersonal experiences (Hartgerink et al., 2015; Nida & Williams, 2017; Williams & Jarvis, 2006; Zadro et al., 2004).

text.text: Importantly, these effects emerged not only during severe exclusion but also during subtle exclusion, suggesting that relatively modest reductions in reciprocal social interaction were sufficient to alter adolescents' perceptions of their social experiences.
This sensitivity to varying levels of exclusion is particularly noteworthy because day-to-day peer interactions often involve subtle rather than overt forms of exclusion.

Although previous immersive VR paradigms have demonstrated that ostracism effects can be elicited in immersive virtual environments (Kassner et al., 2012), and have been used to investigate peer-exclusion, emotion regulation, and social support in children and adolescents (De Luca et al., 2026; Stallmann et al., 2023), the present findings extend this literature in two important ways.

text.text: VR provides a means of examining sensitivity to varied levels of social exclusion, allowing investigators to distinguish responses to subtle and severe exclusion within a single immersive paradigm.

Second, by applying this paradigm in a clinically relevant sample, the present findings provide new insight into how adolescents with CD subjectively experience and interpret socially meaningful exclusion, an area that has received comparatively little experimental attention.
Together, these findings highlight the importance of paradigms capable of detecting responses to both subtle and overt forms of social exclusion.

By providing an ecologically valid platform for investigating multidimensional social-affective functioning, Interact VR offers a novel approach for examining the subjective experiences of adolescents with CD.

In addition, the consistent differences between the subtle exclusion condition and the inclusion and severe inclusion conditions suggest some incremental improvement over the traditional task as studies applying

Cyberball with the three-condition design of the current study produce inconsistent, and often null, differences between subtle (sometime referred to as ambiguous rejection) and severe exclusion conditions (e.g., Chernyak et al., 2010; Sandstrom et al., 2017).

text.text: The emotional profile evoked by the Interact VR conditions was also consistent with the broader social exclusion literature.
The pattern of discrete emotional responses further supports the construct validity of Interact VR as a paradigm for eliciting meaningful emotional responses to social exclusion.

As social exclusion increased, participants had a progressively greater probability of reporting sadness, anger, and disgust, alongside reduced happiness, demonstrating that increasing social exclusion elicited distinct patterns of emotional responding.

This pattern is consistent with theoretical models of social rejection, which propose that threats to social acceptance and belonging evoke differentiated emotional responses rather than a unitary experience of distress (Leary et al., 2006; Richman & Leary, 2009).

text.text: Our findings are also consistent with empirical evidence indicating that Cyberball rejection elicits the greatest state emotion increases in anger and decreases in positive affect (e.g., Peterson et al., 2011; Widiastuti et al., 2026).

text.text: We also found that the likelihood of reporting fear or surprised remained unchanged despite increasing severity of exclusion.

These findings are generally consistent with work suggesting that social rejection does not consistently effect fear or surprise, although the published evidence comparing these specific emotions across conditions of experimentally manipulated social rejection is sparse (e.g., Arango-de-Montis et al., 2024; Lawrence et al., 2011).

text.text: Interact VR thus appears to effectively evoke and capture the emotional consequences of social exclusion, rather than simply inducing a broad negative affect.

These discrete emotional responses provide important insight into how adolescents with CD subjectively experienced varying levels of social exclusion, representing an important component of social-affective functioning.
One curious pattern of findings was the divergent pattern observed across the three dimensions of affective experience.
As social exclusion intensified, adolescents with CD reported increasingly negative affective valence and reduced perceived control but lower subjective arousal.
Theoretical models of ostracism predict that increasingly aversive experiences of social exclusion evoke progressively stronger emotional reactions (Richman & Leary, 2009; Williams, 2007).

text.text: In contrast, participants in our study had a greater probability of reporting emotions that comprise high levels of arousal (e.g., anger, disgust) yet reported lower levels of subjective arousal following rejection.
This pattern of results is likely an artifact of how we measured subjective arousal.
We asked participants to report subjective arousal following each condition on a scale of 1 (Relaxed & Calm) to 10 (Very Excited).
text.formatted: We asked participants to report subjective arousal following each condition on a scale of 1 (Relaxed & Calm) to 10 (Very Excited).

text.text: The framing of this question however may have been interpreted by participants as asking them how excited they were to continue playing with the 'partners' that had just rejected them.

This interpretation is consistent with our finding that the inclusion condition had the highest level of our self-reported arousal measure, which may not have been well understood by our young participants.

Because current diagnostic frameworks define CD primarily in terms of observable behavior, comparatively less is known about how adolescents with CD subjectively experience and respond to socially meaningful interpersonal interactions.

The present study provides initial validation evidence that Interact VR offers a promising, ecologically valid paradigm for examining such processes, providing an experimentally controlled platform for investigating how adolescents with CD subjectively experience and respond to varying levels of social exclusion.

Adolescence is characterized by heightened sensitivity to peer evaluation and social status, and experimental studies using Cyberball have consistently demonstrated that social exclusion influences adolescents' mood, psychological need satisfaction, and neural systems involved in social evaluation and distress (Masten et al., 2009; Ruggieri et al., 2013; Sebastian et al., 2010).

text.text: Given the high prevalence of peer rejection and interpersonal difficulties among adolescents with CD, experimental paradigms capable of examining how these youth subjectively experience socially meaningful interpersonal interactions may provide valuable insight into the social-affective processes that contribute to persistent interpersonal difficulties.

By demonstrating systematic and theoretically coherent responses across multiple domains of social-affective functioning, the present study provides initial validation evidence that Interact VR can be used to investigate social-affective processes that have been difficult to capture using traditional behavioral paradigms.

As such, Interact VR provides an experimentally controlled, standardized, and ecologically valid platform for investigating social-affective processes that cannot be inferred from behavioral symptoms alone.
Importantly, CD is characterized by substantial clinical and behavioral heterogeneity (Fairchild et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Importantly, CD is characterized by substantial clinical and behavioral heterogeneity <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Fairchild et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, it is unlikely that adolescents with CD exhibit a single pattern of social-affective functioning.
Rather, considerable heterogeneity likely exists in how they perceive and respond to socially meaningful interactions.

By providing a standardized yet ecologically valid social context, Interact VR offers a promising platform for characterizing this social-affective heterogeneity beyond observable behavioral symptoms and for determining whether distinct patterns of social-affective functioning are associated with differences in peer functioning, aggression, treatment response, or the persistence of antisocial behavior.

More broadly, Interact VR aligns with the goals outlined by NIMH's RDoC framework, which emphasizes the need for experimentally controlled paradigms that provide ecologically valid, developmentally appropriate assessment of dimensional variation in social processes (Cuthbert & Insel, 2013; Morris et al., 2022; National Institute of Mental Health, 2016).

text.text: Interact VR addresses these measurement priorities by systematically varying the severity of social exclusion within an immersive, standardized social environment while providing multidimensional assessment of social-affective functioning.
As such, the paradigm could be integrated with behavioral, self-report, and psychophysiological measures to advance understanding of social-affective functioning in adolescents with CD.

The present study has several notable strengths, including the use of an immersive, experimentally controlled paradigm that systematically varied levels of social exclusion, the examination of multiple dimensions of social-affective functioning, and the focus on a clinically relevant sample of adolescents with CD.
Nevertheless, several limitations should be considered when interpreting these findings.
First, the inclusion condition was always completed before the exclusion conditions to establish a credible social interaction prior to exclusion.

Although this sequencing was necessary to establish a credible social interaction prior to exclusion and thereby enhanced the ecological plausibility of the paradigm, comparisons between inclusion and exclusion cannot be fully separated from potential order, acclimation, or carryover effects.
However, because the subtle and severe exclusion conditions were randomized, differences between these conditions are less likely to reflect sequence effects.
Future studies should examine alternative sequencing approaches or directly evaluate potential order effects while preserving the progressive nature of the social interaction.

text.text: Such work will be essential for establishing the paradigm as a robust research tool for investigating social-affective functioning in adolescents with CD.

The present study provides initial validation evidence that Interact VR is an ecologically valid paradigm for examining social-affective functioning across varying levels of social exclusion in adolescents with CD.

Subtle and severe levels of exclusion across were distinguished across multiple domains of social-affective functioning, including perceived social regard, belonging, meaningful existence, discrete emotional responses, and broader affective dimensions.

Together, these findings demonstrate that Interact VR captures social exclusion as a multidimensional social-affective experience, eliciting theoretically coherent patterns of responding across multiple domains of social-affective functioning.

By capturing these converging patterns within a single immersive paradigm, Interact VR provides a richer characterization of adolescents' experiences of social exclusion than traditional behavioral paradigms alone.
Because current diagnostic frameworks define CD primarily in terms of observable behavior, the social-affective processes underlying social dysfunction remain less understood.

The present validation study demonstrates that Interact VR provides a promising, ecologically valid, and experimentally controlled platform for examining these processes, offering a means of moving beyond behavioral characterization to investigate how adolescents with CD subjectively experience and respond to social exclusion.

By providing an experimentally controlled yet socially meaningful platform for investigating these processes, Interact VR lays the foundation for future research aimed at advancing the understanding of social functioning and informing more developmentally sensitive models of CD.
